12.0.0.en: 1 And Job answered and said, 2 "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you. 3 But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these? 4 I am as one made a mockery to his neighbour. He called upon God, and he answered him: the just upright man is laughed to scorn. 5 For the one tried there is contempt in the thoughts of him that is at ease, prepared for them whose foot slippeth.

12.1.0.en: "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you" [2].

12.1.1.en: Job rebukes his friends because they are not wise:

12.1.2.en: First: because wisdom has fled from their harshness. This rebuke is directed to everyone who is proud and despises his brother, especially in the time of his sufferings. Such a person does not know how to set limits to rebuke, just as he does not know how to choose the right time. "A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity: but a babbler and a fool will regard no time" (Sir 20:7).

12.1.3.en: Second: because they imagine themselves a people who monopolize wisdom, and that their judgment is the best and highest, by which every person is measured and judged. Therefore the Holy Bible warns us against falling into this delusion, when we count ourselves wise in arrogance and pride. "Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil" (Prov 3:7). "Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him" (Prov 26:12). "The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out" (Prov 28:11). "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches" (Jer 9:23).

12.1.4.en: * Be a fool in the world, as the Apostle directs you, and you will become wise. Do not be partial (to your own opinion) and do not pass judgment from yourself in what you ask about, but always show obedience with all simplicity and faith. Only take care that these matters be holy, profitable and wise, as they proclaim the law of God and disclose the opinion of your spiritual father in those matters.

12.1.5.en: St. John Cassian Third: because they thought that after their death wisdom would die, and all mankind without them would be counted ignorant. After their sun sets, the world falls into the darkness of ignorance.

12.1.6.en: It is folly to imagine that our death causes a great loss, and that we cannot be dispensed with, for God is able to raise up after us one more capable than we. The death of the wise and the righteous does not mean the death of wisdom and righteousness.

12.1.7.en: Fourth: immoderation in conduct under the cover of wisdom turns even what is good into destruction rather than edification. "Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?" (Eccl 7:16)

12.1.8.en: Fifth: Pope Gregory (the Great) and other Fathers see that Job's friends represent the heretics who rely on their human wisdom and their intellectual, material and social resources in arrogance and haughtiness, despising the spiritual mind of the Church.

12.1.9.en: "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" (1 Cor 1:20)

12.1.10.en: "Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" (1 Cor 3:18).

12.1.11.en: "Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom" (Jas 3:13).

12.1.12.en: * Job speaks in astonishment... as though he says: Is the honor of rational beings really bound up with you?

12.1.13.en: Do you know the wisdom of God concerning sinners and the righteous?

12.1.14.en: Is it fitting for men to know it?

12.1.15.en: Do you know that God tests the righteous (Sir 2:5), while confirming His longsuffering toward sinners? (Sir 2:11).

12.1.16.en: This is the reason that some are in prosperity and others in trial, for in the case of some, longsuffering leads them back to repentance (Ezek 33:11), while for others the struggle (with trial) supplies them with the crown (1 Cor 9:25). If you understood this you would no longer condemn the righteous man who is in trial, nor count the sinner who is in prosperity as if he were righteous. But let each one be judged according to his works. If you knew this, it would not be fitting for you to speak in this manner in the judgment to come...

12.1.17.en: Can the wisdom of this work die with men? Where is astrology? Where is the divination by watching the flight of birds? Where is sorcery? Where is soothsaying? In these you find the defiled wisdom, devised from the folly of deceit. Or does such wisdom remain alive here below?

12.1.18.en: The wisdom of God, on the contrary, accompanies him who seeks it, for it accords with training in the knowledge of God and His law. By this a man sees two things very clearly: the glory of God, and the power of the Law given to us.

12.1.19.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * All the wicked, and all the heretics, are not afraid to teach in a harsh tone those who are better than they, since they see everyone as inferior to themselves. But the holy Church calls every one who is haughty in mind, and every self-assured person, to renew him with the spirit of sound-mindedness by being joined together in equality. Job, who is a member of this same holy Church, when he saw his friends in pride uttering grand words in teaching, answered them, saying: "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you" [2]. For what does a man who thinks he surpasses all men in the power of reason do but boast that he is "the only man"? It often happens that the mind swells with pride in loftiness, despising all men and admiring itself. For man's flattering of himself springs from delusion, in folly, being deceived by himself, as one who alone has wisdom. He thinks about everything he says and prizes everything he utters, admiring himself and belittling the words of others. So whoever thinks that he alone is truly wise is confined within his own narrow self.

12.1.21.en: * It is clear that the false apostles had the gift of eloquence which Paul lacked. But it means nothing as long as the substance of the preaching stands, and they cast a shadow over the glory of the Cross, for this (eloquence) is nothing but an attractive appearance.

12.1.22.en: * Here Paul accuses the false teachers not only of boasting excessively, but also of claiming credit for the labors of others.

12.1.23.en: St. John Chrysostom * (Satan) invented heresies and schisms in order to destroy the faith, corrupt the truth, and shatter unity. And since he is unable to keep us in the dark paths of the new error, he draws us into a new maze of deception.

12.1.24.en: He hunts men away from the Church itself, and when they think they have drawn near to the light and fled from the night of the world, he plunges them into a new darkness of which they are unaware.

12.1.25.en: And although they do not hold to the Gospel and the order of Christ and His law, they claim that they are in the light through the deceptive flatteries of the enemy, he of whom the Apostle says that he transforms himself into an angel of light and adorns his servants as servants of righteousness.

12.1.26.en: They call night day, and death salvation, and despair hope, and treachery faithfulness, and antichrist Christ, and he undermines the truth by deceit by presenting the truth in a false guise.

12.1.27.en: This is what happens, my brethren, when we do not return to the fountain of truth, when we do not look to the Head and keep the teaching that comes from heaven.

12.1.28.en: St. Cyprian "But I have understanding as well as you."

12.2.0.en: "yea, who knoweth not such things as these?" [3]

12.2.1.en: It was not by way of boasting that he said to them, "I have understanding as well as you," but he wanted them not to fall into arrogance, as though the knowledge of the divine mysteries concerning God's wisdom in His care for creation and in His dealing with the wicked and the righteous were confined to them and no one else. He is not less than they in knowledge, and perhaps many have the same knowledge.

12.2.2.en: His aim here is to suppress their pride, not to boast of his knowledge and be proud. It reads in the Septuagint: [But I have a heart as well as you].

12.2.3.en: * [But I have a heart as well as you] [3 LXX]. He says: [I know how to think exactly as you do, and moreover I have the heart of a man like you. But you have darkened your hearts, while I have made mine fruitful by the law of God. This is the reason that, though I have a heart like yours, I see what you cannot see. So I am not surprised if you mock me].

12.2.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you" [3]. Who is ignorant of how great the blessed Job was, and that his experience surpassed the knowledge of his friends? Now in order to correct their pride he affirms that he is not less than they, and lest he should sin and exceed the bounds of his humility, he reserved for himself that he is higher than they.

12.2.6.en: How beautiful it is for a man to feel the fellowship of mankind in the enjoyment of reason and thought and also of emotions and heart, each as God has granted him, for the glory of God and the edification of man and of the community. But what distinguishes one from another is the sanctification of what he has received from the hands of God by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, and the kindling of these gifts with faithfulness and diligence according to God's will. This sanctification will not be accomplished by compulsion against our will, nor is it enjoyed by anyone but the humble.

12.2.7.en: * God gave the rational nature the grace of free will, and bestowed on man the ability to determine what he wills, so that goodness may dwell in our life, not by compulsion or involuntarily but as the result of free choice. Our enjoyment of free will leads us to discover clear truths. In the nature of things, if anyone misuses such free will, then according to the words of the Apostle such a person becomes an inventor of evil things (Rom 30:1). Everyone who is of God is counted a brother to us, but he who refuses to share in good works does so by his own full will.

12.2.8.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * May the Lord God give us the grace of humility, which uproots man from many diseases and keeps him from many trials.

12.2.9.en: Abba Dorotheus of Gaza * Whoever knows the frailty of human nature gains experience of the power of God.

12.2.10.en: Abba Maximus the Confessor "I am as one made a mockery (a laughingstock) to his neighbour."

12.2.11.en: "He called upon God, and he answered him."

12.3.0.en: "the just upright man is laughed to scorn (a laughingstock)" [4].

12.3.1.en: Job discovered that they treated him with great disdain, belittling him and trampling on him as though he were the object of their mockery or amusement rather than supporting him in earnest.

12.3.2.en: Indeed they came to comfort him and counsel him, but their way of counseling turned into biting criticism, and they wronged him in his affliction. Job might have accepted this from enemies gloating over him, but to come from dear friends is hard to bear. "For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance" (Ps 55:12-13), and in this Job was a type of the Lord Christ, of whom it is said: "What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends" (Zech 13:6). What increased his wound was not only that they were his friends, but that they were elders, leaders of the people and religious men. He wished that they would pray for him before God and He would answer them, and that they would seek counsel from God and offer words of consolation from God instead of the exceedingly painful rebukes. This is the lot of the prophets and the apostles and all men of God and all the righteous, to be mocked even by those close to them.

12.3.3.en: * The more the saints acquire love for God, the more they endure everything for His sake.

12.3.4.en: St. Augustine * [Yes, the just and perfect man is delivered up to mockery] [4]. Not everyone mocks him, but sinners mock him (Wis 5:3); the sensible do not mock him, but the drunken, for it is the habit of the drunken to mock the sensible. This is true, for children often mock old men. So the sinner mocks the righteous (Jer 20:7-8), for they sow in tears and pains (Ps 126:5-6). The sinner does not think of the coming fruits, and that the righteous passes from tears to joy, and from pain to surpassing honor, and that the sorrows of the righteous last only for a time (2 Cor 4:17-18).

12.3.5.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * While the wicked rebuke the souls of the good, they show those whom they rebuke to be witnesses against them. While the groaning soul confines itself to prayer, it is united within to hear the Most High, and that by the very thing it suffers from the self-assurance of men... For the mockery of his fellow creatures makes him near to God (His friend), he whose innocence makes him a stranger to the evil of his fellow creatures...

12.3.6.en: It is the wisdom of the righteous that makes them seek nothing of outward show, but perceive the meanings in the words; they love the truth as it is, avoiding vain pride.

12.3.7.en: They do not practice good works in order to bear evil (pride), finding in it more delight than in practicing them.

12.3.8.en: They do not avenge the injury, counting every insult for the sake of the truth a gain!

12.3.9.en: But this simplicity of the righteous is laughed at (by the wicked) with contempt, and the wise of this world count the goodness of purity folly. For without doubt everything practiced in innocence they count as stupidity, and the practice of all the laws of truth appears to them as weakness in comparison with fleshly wisdom... But in the eyes of the hidden Judge such a one (marked by innocence) is radiant with virtues, full of splendor springing from the merits of his life. He fears to be honored, he does not shrink when he is despised, he trains his body in chastity, fruitful in love alone in the soul... He rejoices when he is reviled, has compassion from his heart on the afflicted, and rejoices at the success of the good as if it were his own. He considers carefully the provision of the holy Word in the heart, and when tested he is found inexperienced in giving a double answer. He is a lamp, because he shines within, and he is mocked because he does not shine outwardly. Within he gleams with the flame of love, and outwardly he shines without the splendor of (vain) glory. He shines and is despised, he who gleams with virtue and is counted contemptible.

12.3.10.en: Thus St. David was looked upon with contempt by his father when he refused to present him before the eyes of the prophet Samuel, when he presented his seven sons to receive the gift of anointing. And when the prophet asked him whether he had brought all his sons, he answered with contempt: "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep" (1 Sam 16:11). And when he brought him and he was chosen, he heard the words: "man looketh on the eyes, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7).

12.3.11.en: And also the skilled preacher lessened the glory of his apostleship in the eyes of men, saying: [nor did we use authority when we might have been burdensome as the apostles of Christ, but we made ourselves little children among you] (see 1 Thess 2:6-7).

12.4.0.en: "For the one tried there is contempt in the thoughts of him that is at ease, prepared for them whose foot slippeth" [5].

12.4.1.en: It appears in the English translation:

12.4.2.en: He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease.)Job 12:5 KJV)

12.4.3.en: As though he says that he whose foot slips falls into troubles even if he was formerly like a lamp. He is looked upon as a lamp that has gone out, and as a wick that we throw on the ground and trample with our feet.

12.4.4.en: This is what embitters Job's soul, that those in prosperity and fullness despise those who are tried and suffering and hungry.

12.4.5.en: * [At the appointed time he is ready to die by the blows of the stranger; he sees his house destroyed by the wicked] [5 LXX].

12.4.6.en: "At the appointed time," what kind of time? As God appoints the time, He who changes the hours and the times according to His will, moving each one here and there.

12.4.7.en: He is the One who knows the limits of men immersed in trial, and how far they can bear the trial.

12.4.8.en: He sets a time [to die by the blows of the enemies], that is, the righteous are ill-treated by the wicked. That is, He will declare by what dealings the wicked wrong the righteous, and how they pass their life in luxury. But as for the righteous, it is clear how they live in perseverance (Jas 5:11), and how they endure sorrows here on earth.

12.4.9.en: It is not at random that God allows the wicked to destroy the houses of the righteous, but He does not forsake the righteous, nor allow things beyond their ability... For they suffer no harm from this destruction, because the dwellings of the present life and the earthly tents are destroyed (2 Cor 5:1-2), even if they are not plundered.

12.4.10.en: This then is what we believe, that we experience something of destruction, but find in it our gain very clearly. For we receive the reward for perseverance and the recompense for our diligence, and in place of our earthly dwelling we inherit a heavenly dwelling where we live among the angels and archangels.

12.4.11.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The despised lamp, which is subject to mockery on earth, shines by the judgment of heaven. Therefore it is rightly added: [prepared at the appointed time]. Concerning this time the psalmist says: "For I appoint a time, I judge uprightly" (Ps 75:2). And the Truth declares in the Gospel: [for my time is not yet fulfilled] (Jn 7:6). And Peter says: "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things" (Acts 3:21).

12.4.13.en: St. Mar Aphrahat the Persian Sage tells us how one of the wise men stumbled at Christianity because of the severity of the persecution the Christians suffer, without God intervening to rescue them, and what the saint's answer to him was, as he presented living examples from the Old Testament showing that God allows affliction for His beloved ones in order that they may be glorified at the appointed time.

12.4.14.en: * It happened one day that a man called a wise man among the Jews asked me: Jesus, who is called your Teacher, wrote that if any one of you has faith like a grain of mustard seed, you say to this mountain, Remove, and it is removed from before you, and it is lifted up and falls into the sea, and it obeys you (a) (Mt 17:19; 21:22). And it is clear that there is not one wise man among all your people whose prayer is heard, so as to ask God to put an end to those who persecute you. So it is evident that this was written for you: [nothing shall be impossible unto you] (b).

12.4.15.en: * And when I saw him blaspheming and speaking against the Way, my mind was troubled, and I realized that he did not know the interpretation of the words he had quoted and said to me. Then on my part I asked him about sayings from the Law and the Prophets, and said to him: Do you trust that even when you are scattered God is with you...? For He said to Israel: [Even in the lands of your enemies I will not forget you, nor break my covenant with you] (see Lev 26:44).

12.4.16.en: I answered him: [Well, I hear this from you, that God is with you. But I also speak words against you], for the prophet says to Israel as from the mouth of God: [When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee. For I am the LORD thy God] (see Isa 43:2-3). Thus is there not one wise man among you, righteous and good, out of all the people, who may pass through the sea and live without drowning, and cross the river without being overwhelmed, and who is able to walk on fire and not be burned, and the flame not consume him? And if you offer me an explanation I do not accept it from you, just as you do not accept the interpretation of the words you asked me about.

12.4.17.en: * Jacob was persecuted, and Esau was the persecutor. Jacob received the blessings and the birthright, while Esau was deprived of both.

12.4.18.en: * Joseph was persecuted, and his brothers were the persecutors. Joseph was glorified, and his persecutors bowed down to him, and his dreams and visions were fulfilled.

12.4.19.en: Joseph the persecuted was a type of Jesus the persecuted.

12.4.20.en: Joseph's father clothed him with a coat of many colors, and Jesus' Father clothed Him with a body from the Virgin.

12.4.21.en: Joseph's father loved him more than his brothers, and Jesus is the dear beloved of His Father.

12.4.22.en: Joseph saw visions and dreamed dreams, and the visions and the prophets were fulfilled in Jesus.

12.4.23.en: Joseph was a shepherd with his brothers, and Jesus is the Chief Shepherd.

12.4.24.en: When his father sent him to visit his brothers, they saw Joseph coming and plotted to kill him, and when the Father sent Jesus to visit His brothers they said: [This is the heir; come, let us kill him] (Mt 21:38).

12.4.25.en: Joseph's brothers cast their brother into the pit, and Jesus was brought down by His brothers to dwell among the dead.

12.4.26.en: Joseph came up from the pit, and Jesus rose from among the dead.

12.4.27.en: * Moses was also persecuted as Jesus was persecuted.

12.4.28.en: When Moses was born they hid him from his persecutors lest they kill him, and when Jesus was born they fled with Him to Egypt so that Herod His persecutor might not kill Him.

12.4.29.en: In the days when Moses was born they were drowning the children in the river, and at the birth of Jesus the children of Bethlehem and its surroundings were killed.

12.4.30.en: To Moses God said: [for all the men are dead which sought thy life] (Ex 4:19). And to Joseph the angel said in Egypt: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life" (Mt 2:20).

12.4.31.en: Moses brought his people out of the service of Pharaoh, and Jesus delivered the peoples from the service of Satan.

12.4.32.en: Moses was brought up in Pharaoh's house, and Jesus was brought up in Egypt when Joseph fled with Him there.

12.4.33.en: * Joshua the son of Nun was persecuted as Jesus our Savior was persecuted.

12.4.34.en: Joshua the son of Nun was persecuted by the unclean peoples, and Jesus our Savior was persecuted by the ignorant people.

12.4.35.en: Joshua the son of Nun took the inheritance from his persecutors and gave it to his people, and Jesus our Savior took the inheritance from His persecutors and gave it to foreign peoples.

12.4.36.en: Joshua the son of Nun stopped the sun and the moon and took vengeance on the peoples who persecuted him, and Jesus our Savior made the sun set in the middle of the day, to put to shame the persecuting people who crucified Him.

12.4.37.en: Joshua the son of Nun distributed the inheritance to his people, and Jesus our Savior promised to give the peoples the land of life.

12.4.38.en: * These memoirs which I write to you, my beloved, concerning Jesus who was persecuted, and the righteous who were persecuted, are for the sake of those who are persecuted today for the sake of the persecuted Jesus, that they may find rest. For He wrote to us and comforted us Himself: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you. They persecute you because ye are not of the world, even as I am not of the world" (see Jn 19:15, 20; 14:17).

12.4.39.en: St. Mar Aphrahat the Persian Sage

12.5.s.en: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

12.5.0.en: 6 "The tabernacles of the spoilers are at rest, and they that provoke God are secure; they bring their god in their hand! 7 But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: 8 Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. 9 Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the LORD hath wrought this? 10 In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind. 11 Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?

12.5.1.en: "The tabernacles of the spoilers (robbers) are at rest, and they that provoke God are secure; they bring their god in their hand!" [6]

12.5.2.en: We should not wonder if we see the wicked living in ease and abundance, their life appearing successful, lacking nothing, mocking the believers who are tried and suffer affliction. They are like the grass that mocks the trees in the winter season when the green leaves have fallen from them and they appear lifeless as though they would never bear fruit, fit only as fuel for the fire. But for everything there is a time appointed by God. Soon the grass dries up, and when the spring season comes we see that the grass has gone and perhaps another has taken its place, while the trees that seemed dry bear leaves and fruit and have a special beauty. So Job looked at his friends who had made him the object of their mockery, and sang that for everything with God there is a time.

12.5.3.en: Job objected to the principle which his friends held, that the wicked cannot prosper long in the world, but calamities will surely come upon them suddenly. And he determined that God has His wisdom in His dealing with men, and He may postpone the recompense or punishment to the other world. Therefore he says that the tents of robbers are sometimes prosperous; they practice blasphemy, violence and the persecution of others, and yet they are successful. Perhaps he refers here to the Sabeans and the Chaldeans who plundered his possessions and yet appear to be successful.

12.5.4.en: It is not strange that those who practice evil are like arrogant robbers who care nothing for their relationship with God. They plunder others by treachery and betrayal, and fear no harm that may come upon them.

12.5.5.en: * "Yet let not the wicked expect to go out unpunished" [6 LXX]. May no one err in estimating the longsuffering of God, or fail to take the coming judgment into account.

12.5.6.en: May no one believe that the just Judge leaves the deeds of the wicked without chastisement.

12.5.7.en: Let him learn a lesson from the judgments that came upon Pharaoh (Ex 14:4) and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:31-33) and Jezebel (2 Kgs 9:7-10), and the Amalekites (Bar 3:27-28) and the sons of Korah (Num 16:31), and the company of Dathan (Num 26:9-10) and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24-25), and all the rest of the nations. For looking at these wicked nations and how they despised God's longsuffering makes us pause and fear the punishment that may come upon the likes of them.

12.5.8.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem St. Augustine often reassures us that although the wheat is found mixed with the chaff in this world without the chaff being burned, this will not harm the wheat nor deprive it of its crown, for the time will come to separate it from the chaff, when the chaff is burned in the fire.

12.5.9.en: * This chaff does not destroy those who are the wheat of the Lord, who are few if compared with the others, yet they are a great multitude. God's elect, who are gathered from the ends of the world, from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other (Mt 24:31), do not perish. The elect cry out saying: "Help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men" (Ps 12:1). And the Lord says to them: [he that shall endure unto the end (where evil is bound), the same shall be saved] (Mt 24:13).]

12.5.10.en: St. Augustine It is not for us to judge and separate the wheat from the tares, and the vessels unto honor from those unto dishonor, but it is also fitting for us to be assured that the wheat is not neglected by God because of the tares, nor do the honored vessels lose their honor because of those unto dishonor, for the Apostle says: "The Lord knoweth them that are his."

12.5.11.en: * It is not for the sake of the chaff that the wheat perishes (Mt 3:12), nor because of the bad fish is anything from the net not taken into the vessels (Mt 13:47)... He has already predestinated us before we were born, promising us with certainty: "Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified" (Rom 8:30). As he also says: [even if the seed is hidden in the chaff, it is known to the owner of the field. Let no one fear, when he is a seed, even if he is in the midst of chaff, for the eyes of Him who sows us are not deceived.]

12.6.0.en: St. Augustine "But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee" [7].

12.6.1.en: Job shows that what these three counted as wisdom to boast of is nothing but natural knowledge, by which all creation is taught, even the beasts and the birds of the air.

12.6.2.en: * He says: ask even those without speech (Job 12:7); they may lack language, but they point in a natural way, for they know their Creator, and confess that He is their Maker, and that He is the secret of their existence. Now ask the beasts: at whose command did Balaam's ass speak (Num 22:28)? So ask the birds of the heaven: why did the ravens feed Elijah (1 Kgs 17:4-6)?

12.6.3.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * If you are in the bounds of the night, contemplating the captivating beauty of the stars, you see the Artist who designed them and adorned the heaven with these roses. If you are in the early morning, you learn of the wonders of the day, and through the visible things you reach the invisible.

12.6.4.en: * Let the splendor of these visible things be a reason for us to understand the invisible, which is above all earthly beauty. And let the wonder of these limited sensible things lift us to perceive the loftiness of Him who is eternal, unlimited, whose might surpasses the grasp of our minds and understandings.

12.6.5.en: * Has the day passed? Give thanks to Him who gave us the sun for the service of our daily work, and gives us fire to light the night and serve our other needs in life. May the night also suggest to us what moves us to prayer.

12.6.6.en: When you look at the heaven and see the beauty of the stars, pray to the Lord of all visible things, the Creator of the world, who in wisdom made them all (Ps 104:24).

12.6.7.en: And when you see all nature sunk in sleep, again bow down to Him who even against our will frees us from the pressure of continual labor, and by a little interval of rest restores us again to the activity of our strength.

12.6.8.en: Do not allow the whole night to be for sleep; do not allow half of your life to pass fruitlessly in dull slumber and torpor. Rather divide the night between sleep and prayer. And let your very light sleep be exercises in godliness. For our dreams during sleep are often reflections of our thoughts in the day.

12.7.0.en: St. Basil the Great "Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee" [8].

12.7.1.en: All the dumb creatures bear witness that the big devours the small, like the fish, and the strong preys on the small, like the beasts of prey. Had sin not entered, none of this would have happened, but [the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb] (Isa 11:6).

12.7.2.en: * Who can know the manner of the eternal begetting? The Father who begot is not in a way that any man can understand, but He alone can understand.

12.7.3.en: For we know that we should not tell the manner in which He begot Him, but we insist that it is not in this manner; and not only are we ignorant of the birth of the Son from the Father, but we are ignorant of every created nature.

12.7.4.en: "Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee" (Job 12:8). Although you ask all the things that are on the earth, they are unable to tell you. For the earth cannot tell of the essence of Him who fashioned it as a potter and made it. And not only the earth but the sun also... and the heaven also does not declare it... nor the heaven of heavens.

12.7.5.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * [Ask the fishes of the sea] Who commanded the whale to swallow Jonah (Jon 1:17; 2:10)?

12.7.6.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * There are migratory fish, as though they migrate by collective decision, at a particular signal, to strange regions. When the time of their breeding comes, they depart, these from one gulf and those from another, driven by a general natural law, hastening to the Black Sea. You see these fish at their departure like a torrent pouring through the Bosphorus toward the Black Sea. Who moved them? And where is the king who presides over them? And the orders posted in the public squares, appointing the time of the journey? And where are the commanders? You see divine providence accomplishing everything and caring for the lowest of creatures. The fish do not resist the law of God, but we human beings transgress His teachings.

12.7.7.en: So do not despise the fish because they are mute and speechless, and fear lest you be less reasonable than they when you transgress the commands of your Creator.

12.7.8.en: Listen to the fish, which lack nothing but speech, and their conduct tells you: the preservation of the species drives them to undertake this long journey. They have no understanding, but a natural law deeply rooted in their instinct drives them to what they must do. They say: Come, let us go to the Black Sea... its water is sweeter than other waters, and the sun above it is less hot so that it does not absorb all its sweet water; therefore the fish go up the rivers and keep away from the seas, and prefer the Black Sea to receive and rear their young in it, and when each has accomplished his purpose there, all return the way they came. Why? As though by their conduct they said to us: [The Black Sea is shallow, exposed to violent storms, with few refuges, and often turned upside down by the raging winds and stirred up by heaps of sand. And besides it is cold in winter, because of the great rivers that flow into it], so the fish leave it after having benefited from it in summer, and hasten their return to the warmth of deep waters and the regions that have the warmth of the sun, and rest in a calm sea far from the fierce north wind.

12.7.9.en: I have seen this scene and marveled at the all-embracing wisdom of God.

12.7.10.en: If the speechless beasts submit to hidden instincts, and know how to provide for their livelihood, and if the fish know what they should choose and what they should avoid, what shall we say, we who have been honored with a rational nature, and cultured by the Law, and called by the divine promises, and have drunk in wisdom by the Holy Spirit? Do we order our affairs with less good sense than the fish?

12.7.11.en: Do they learn to provide for some things before they happen, while we, on the contrary, hardly care, and spend our life in bestial pleasures?

12.7.12.en: The fish crosses all the seas in search of some of its benefits, and what do you say, if you live in sluggishness and idleness? Let no one plead ignorance, for in us is a natural mind that shows us the fitness of good and makes us shrink from harmful acts.

12.8.0.en: St. Basil the Great "Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the LORD hath wrought this?" [9]

12.8.1.en: Every rational being, or even irrational, can perceive that God is its Creator and that He is the One who sustains it.

12.9.0.en: "In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind" [10].

12.9.1.en: * [Is not the life of every living thing in his hand?] Why do all the young ravens call upon Him (Ps 147:9)?

12.9.2.en: Why do the lions' whelps seek their food from God (Ps 104:21)?

12.9.3.en: If these creatures take their Creator into account, how much more is it fitting for us whom He brought into existence! We who are ignorant that "the breath of all mankind" is in God's hand, He who from the beginning breathed into us the breath of life (Gen 2:7) (c). David showed this in his prophetic songs: [Thou takest away their breath, and they return to their dust] (Ps 104:29).

12.9.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "The hand" indicates "power"... He gives the soul the power to give life to the body, and on the other hand He quickens the soul to the extent that it attains the understanding of eternity.

12.9.6.en: * No being is to be credited with its own existence. You alone have not received your existence from another. All of us, that is, all creation, did not exist before we were created. The cause of our existence is the will of the Creator.

12.9.7.en: * The truth of our existence is not the fruit of the merit of our works, but is grace from our Creator.

12.9.8.en: * (Concerning the rational creation) Whatever goodness is found in it is not goodness by nature, but a good gift from its Creator... For the Creator gave it reason, and gave it freedom of movement by free will, so that the good in it might be counted as its own good, by its keeping free will.

12.9.9.en: * No one, whether Jew or Gentile, is without this law that is in men by nature. God gave man all the feelings and senses by which he can struggle to remain in virtue and grow in it. Besides this, God implanted in him the power of reason, by which he perceives what he ought to do and what he ought to avoid. God gave this to all alike.

12.10.0.en: Origen "Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?" [11]

12.10.1.en: It is fitting for the ear not to believe everything it hears, but to distinguish between truth and falsehood, as the mouth distinguishes between sweet and bitter. And if the ear, like the mouth, needs to discern what is set before it, whether in hearing or in food, is it not fitting for man to bear a spirit of discernment, to know sound teachings from unsound (1 Cor 10:15; 11:13)?

12.10.2.en: * He is not speaking of the ear of the body, but the ear of the spirit. With bodily ears we hear the sounds of words, but with the inward ears we distinguish thought and words. Likewise [the palate (especially taste) tasteth his meat], that is, it appreciates it with regard to its pleasantness. So the palate of the spirit discerns its benefit.

12.10.3.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [For the mind νοῦς (nous) discerns words]... If God gives us the palate to discern the taste of food, He also gives us the mind to make our decisions, and time allows us to seek understanding.

12.10.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * There is one judge who oversees the inner, that is, the power of discernment of the mind, but through fitting ways that keep the five senses distinct. God works wonders, so the eye cannot hear, nor the ear see, nor the mouth smell, nor the nose taste, nor the hands smell. While all these work through the powers of the one mind, yet no sense can practice other than what the Creator has assigned to it. And so through these outward bodily arrangements, it is left to us to gather them inwardly in a spiritual way...

12.10.5.en: While there is one wisdom dwelling in one man less than in another... yet in itself it carries no differences among them, but by it we practice various and different operations, so one receives the gift of wisdom, another the gift of knowledge, another tongues, another the gift of healing...

12.10.6.en: The blessed Job condemns the inexperience of his friends, and the insolence of everyone who swells up claiming to have been taught in wisdom. For to know something about God is one thing, and to taste what you know with understanding is another.

12.10.8.en: * There is not one virtue that we can obtain by our human effort unless divine grace helps us. And we see in the Holy Bible that discernment is counted among the gifts of the Spirit, for the Apostle says: "For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit... to another discerning of spirits"...

12.10.9.en: You have seen then how the gift of discernment is not an earthly gift, nor is it a trifling matter, but it is a great gift bestowed by divine grace. If a man does not strive with all zeal after discernment... he will surely err and become like one in the darkness of night and the gloom of obscurity, and he falls not only into snares and passions but errs even in easy matters...

12.10.10.en: Discernment teaches a man to walk in the royal way, not allowing him extremism on the right in virtue, that is, exaggeration and exceeding the bounds of moderation in boldness and insolence, nor allowing him laziness...

12.10.11.en: This is the discernment which the Holy Bible expresses by "the eye" or "the light of the body," as the Savior says: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light. But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.." (Mt 22:6, 23). For it is that which discerns all thoughts and deeds, and sees everything and watches what will happen.

12.10.12.en: So if a man's eye is "evil," that is, not fortified by the voice of wisdom and knowledge, deceived by some errors and arrogance (in worship), it makes our body "full of darkness." Our minds are darkened and our deeds are in the darkness of vice and the gloom of disturbances, and as He says: "If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!" (Mt 23:6).

12.10.13.en: No one can doubt that when "the judgment in matters" in the heart is mistaken, that is, when the heart is full of ignorance, our thoughts and deeds, which are the fruit of discernment and contemplation, are in the darkness of the greatest sin.

12.11.0.en: 12 "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding. 13 With him is wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding. 14 Behold, he breaketh down, and it cannot be built again: he shutteth up a man, and there can be no opening. 15 Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth. 16 With him is strength and understanding: the deceived and the deceiver are his. 17 He leadeth counsellors away captive, and maketh the judges fools. 18 He looseth the girdles of kings, and bindeth their loins with a cord. 19 He leadeth priests away captive, and overthroweth the mighty. 20 He removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the taste of the aged. 21 He poureth contempt upon the nobles, and looseneth the girdle of the strong. 22 He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death. 23 He increaseth the nations, and destroyeth them: he enlargeth the nations, and driveth them out. 24 He taketh away the minds of the chiefs of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilderness where there is no way. 25 They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man.

12.11.1.en: "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding" [12].
